auxiliary_material: Mechanistic insights from mouse models: Inosine directly inhibits the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBA6 in tumor cells, enhancing MHC-I expression and tumour-intrinsic immunogenicity, thereby sensitizing tumors to T-cell-mediated killing. Inosine supplementation synergized with ICB in resistant mouse models (B16-GMCSF, 4T1). Clinical validation of the mechanism: Low UBA6 expression in human tumor tissues was associated with better progression-free survival in melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA4 or anti-PD1, and lower UBA6 levels were found in responders (PR/SD) vs. non-responders (PD) in a small basket trial cohort (n=22). Limitations noted by authors: Direct measurement of inosine in the human clinical cohorts was not performed due to technical challenges (rapid degradation/clearance of adenosine/inosine in plasma), so the human data relies on retrospective metabolomic screening where inosine was one of many metabolites analyzed, and mechanistic validation is primarily preclinical.
outline_action: Document the association between high relative plasma inosine levels and improved OS in nivolumab-treated RCC patients (CheckMate 025). Note the lack of absolute concentration data and the absence of butyrate measurements in human cohorts within this study. Highlight the mechanistic link between inosine, UBA6 inhibition, and enhanced tumor immunogenicity as supporting evidence for why such metabolites matter, even if the precise human physiological concentrations are not provided.
remaining_gap: The gap requires quantitative physiological concentrations (e.g., μM, ng/mL) of key microbial metabolites like inosine and butyrate in human tumor microenvironments or paired serum. While this study provides relative abundance data (high vs. low based on median split) from plasma metabolomics in an RCC cohort, it does not report absolute concentration values for inosine in human samples. Furthermore, the study does not measure butyrate or other short-chain fatty acids in human cohorts, nor does it provide paired serum/tumor tissue measurements for these metabolites. The correlation with ICI response is established for inosine in plasma (relative levels), but the specific quantitative threshold and direct concentration-response relationship remain unreported in this text.
useful_material: The study identifies inosine as a purine metabolite associated with improved overall survival in human renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients treated with nivolumab (anti-PD1). Specifically, higher baseline plasma levels of inosine were correlated with longer median overall survival (33 months vs. 22 months for low levels) in the CheckMate 025 trial cohort (n=743 RCC patients, 394 treated with nivolumab). The study also notes that gut microbiota dysbiosis induced by ICB treatment affects plasma purine metabolite levels, and references prior work linking specific bacterial genera (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium) to inosine production.
